Unrounded vowels come before the dot, rounded after it. Length: long vowels aː uː. Nasality: no nasal vowels.

### Tone, syllables and stress

No phonemic tone.
Syllable shapes (share of syllables in the word-shape model): CV 45%, CVC 25%, CCV 11%, CCVC 8%, V 7%, VC 4%. At most 2 consonant(s) before the vowel and 1 after it.
Stress falls on the first syllable.
Core words average 1.63 syllables (3.4 sounds); 30% of words share their form with another word.

### Allophony

This output records no allophones (the engine stores sounds as phonemes only).

## Orthography

The house romanization in two registers: the full spelling (workbench, one letter or digraph per sound, tone marks) and the book spelling (lossy: no tone, plain vowels, at most one diacritic letter a word).

**Consonants:** m ‹m› · n ‹n› · ɲ ‹ny› · ŋ͡m ‹ngm› · ŋ ‹ng› · p ‹p› · b ‹b› · t̪ ‹t̪› ‹t› · d̪ ‹d̪› ‹d› · t ‹t› · d ‹d› · ʈ ‹ṭ› · k ‹k› · ɡ ‹g› · ʔ ‹'› · tʃ ‹ch› · ʈʂʰ ‹ṭṣ› · ɖʐʰ ‹ḍẓ› · tsʼ ‹ts'› · z̪ ‹z̪› ‹z› · s ‹s› · ʒ ‹zh› · v ‹v› · h ‹h› · j ‹y› · w ‹w› · l̪ ‹l̪› ‹l› · l̥ ‹hl› · l ‹l› · ȴ ‹ľ› · r ‹rr› · ɽ ‹ṛ›

**Vowels:** i ‹i› · u ‹u› · uː ‹uu› · ʊ ‹ù› ‹u› · e ‹e› · ɛ ‹è› ‹e› · ʌ̞ ‹e̞o› ‹eo› · a ‹a› · aː ‹aa›

Where two spellings are given the second is the book spelling.

## Grammar

Basic word order is SVO; it has prepositions. In the noun phrase: possessed before the possessor; noun before the adjective; noun before the demonstrative; noun before the numeral; noun before the relative clause. Overall it is head-initial.
It has a definite article after the noun, an indefinite article, no case marking on nouns, no alignment marking (subject and object are not told apart by form), singular and plural, a system of noun classes.
Verbs mark past, future, progressive and habitual; there are no evidentials. Negation uses a negator before the verb; yes/no questions use a final question particle. Verbs do not agree with their arguments.
Other features: serial verbs; adjectives that behave like verbs; a periphrastic causative; no passive; question words moved to the front; a decimal counting base.
Measured morphology: 15 live grammatical markers, mean bondedness 0.7 (0 free word … 3 fused), 13 paradigm cells, 8 of them with allomorphy.

### Grammar sketch

Built from the typology and the live markers above (planet/language/sentences.py); where the engine tracks no marker for a construction, the form is the word such markers commonly grow from, and the text says so. Examples are glossed by the Leipzig rules (abbreviations under Sample sentences).

**Number.** Nouns mark number: plural: a clitic after the noun (u, from 'all').

| *uw* |
| --- |
| dog |

‘dog’

| *uw=u* |
| --- |
| dog=PL |

‘dogs’

**Case.** Nouns have no case marking. Subject and object are not marked apart: word order tells them. Place and company are said with the plain words 'in' (im), 'at' (naː), 'with' (ʊɽaŋ) as adpositions.

**Gender and noun classes.** Nouns are counted with classifiers: class 1 for a single person, a prefix (i, from 'person'); class 2 for people (plural of persons), a prefix (ku, from 'people'); class 3 for languages, ways and tools, a separate word after the noun (u, from 'tongue').

| *i-san* |
| --- |
| CL1-person |

‘person’

| *u* |
| --- |
| tongue |

‘tongue’

**Tense and aspect.** Verbs mark tense and aspect. Past (PST): a clitic before the verb (iŋ, from 'yesterday'); future (FUT): a separate word before the verb (tul, from 'go'); progressive (PROG): a prefix (tu, from 'walk'); habitual (HAB): a separate word before the verb (ʒimuw, from 'do'). Unmarked: perfective (left to context).

| *in=tulam* |
| --- |
| PST=go |

‘(it) went’

| *tul* | *tulam* |
| --- | --- |
| FUT | go |

‘(it) will go’

| *tu-tulam* |
| --- |
| PROG-go |

‘(it) is going’

**Mood and evidentiality.** No evidential or mood marker is live; statements are unmarked.

**Person agreement.** Verbs do not agree with the subject. Pronoun-like words stand beside the verb (2SG u, 3SG i), on their way to becoming agreement.

**Negation.** Negation is a prefix (ɲi, from 'nothing'); the typology calls it preverbal.

| *ɛ* | *ɲi-ji* | *vun* | *ʒiŋ* |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1SG | NEG-drink | milk | DEF |

‘I do not drink the milk.’ (sentence 6 below)

**Questions.** Yes/no questions use a particle at the end of the clause. Question words move to the front: who iŋi, what ɡju, where tsʼjɛ, when il, how i.

| *nɛiʈul* | *iɽiŋ* | *ʒliluʔuʒen* | *ʒiŋ* | *liʒ* |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 2SG | hear | thunder | DEF | Q |

‘Do you hear the thunder?’ (sentence 4 below)

| *ɡju* | *i-ɡjɛ* | *ʒiŋ* | *nʊ* |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| what | CL1-child | DEF | bring |

‘What does the child bring?’ (sentence 5 below)

**Possession.** The possessor stands after the possessed noun, with no marker. 'Having' is said with 'with' ('my mother is with a dog'; the lane's pick for Grambank's 'neither').

| *uw* | *i-jinaŋ* | *ʒiŋ* |
| --- | --- | --- |
| dog | CL1-man | DEF |

‘the man's dog’

| *i-jɛiwiŋ* | *ɛ* | *ʊɽaŋ* | *ʈuwaːt̪ul* | *aȴ* |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| CL1-mother | 1SG | with | boat | INDF |

‘My mother has a boat.’ (sentence 7 below)

**Relative clauses.** Relative clause after the noun, introduced by the word for 'that' (G055).

| *i-jɛiwiŋ* | *ʒiŋ* | *unub* | *ʒɛi* |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| CL1-woman | DEF | REL | dance |

‘the woman who dances’

**Copula.** There is no copula: a predicate noun stands beside its subject. Adjectives behave like verbs: 'the water is cold' is said as 'the water colds', with the verb's markers.

| *i-jinaŋ* | *unub* | *ibi* | *aȴ* |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| CL1-man | that | merchant | INDF |

‘That man is a merchant.’ (sentence 9 below)

| *t̪ulaŋ* | *ʒiŋ* | *ʒil* |
| --- | --- | --- |
| water | DEF | cold |

‘the water is cold’

### Families a speaker feels

The roots a speaker still feels: a derivation or compound younger than 3 kyr whose parts are still in use (per-word `roots`). 3 families of 3+ words; 15% of the 716 words share a root with another word.

The largest: **finger** *pʊɾuɡlej* (N, coined 20 kyr ago in the cloud giant proto-language); 4 words have it as their main root, 4 contain it.

| meaning | IPA | spelling | roots (main first) | how it was built |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| finger | ʊlaul | ulaul | finger | \*pʊɾuɡlej 'finger' (the cloud giant proto-language, 20 kyr) |
| hand | ʊlaul | ulaul | finger | \*pʊɾuɡlej 'hand' (the cloud giant proto-language, 20 kyr) |
| hold | ʊʈjiŋ | uṭying | finger | \*pʊɾuɡlej 'hand' (the cloud giant proto-language, 20 kyr) → HAND + 'do' = 'hold' (0.5) |
| toe | ʊluŋʊ | ulungu | finger, foot | \*pʊɾuɡlej 'finger' (the cloud giant proto-language, 20 kyr) → FINGER + FOOT = 'toe' (2) |

### Families a historian reconstructs

The roots a historian reconstructs: every word's family as it was when the word was made, carried forward however opaque it has become since (per-word `etym_roots`, the *bher- 'carry' > burden view). 54 families of 3+ words; 50% of the 716 words share a root with another word.

The largest: **flow** *d̪ladzaduw* (V, coined 20 kyr ago in the cloud giant proto-language); 10 words have it as their main root, 19 contain it.

## Sample sentences

Built from this language's own words, word order, markers and agreement (planet/language/sentences.py). Each has the form line (‘-’ an affix boundary, ‘=’ a clitic boundary), a morpheme-by-morpheme gloss, the free translation, then the whole sentence in IPA (after the simple joining rules: a glide between two vowels, a nasal taking the place of a following stop) and in the book spelling. Nothing here is attested speech; it is what the grammar data implies.

**(1)** ‘The woman sees the dog.’

| *i-jɛiwiŋ* | *ʒiŋ* | *uwʌ̞* | *uw* | *ʒiŋ* |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| CL1-woman | DEF | see | dog | DEF |

/ijɛiwiŋ ʒiŋ uwʌ̞ uw ʒiŋ/ · ‹Iyeiwing zhing uweo uw zhing.›

<sub>SVO order</sub>

**(2)** ‘The big dog sleeps in the house.’

| *uw* | *kul* | *ʒiŋ* | *pi* | *im* | *ilan* | *ʒiŋ* |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| dog | big | DEF | sleep | in | house | DEF |

/uw kul ʒiŋ pi im ilan ʒiŋ/ · ‹Uw kul zhing pi im ilan zhing.›

<sub>'in' as a preposition (no LOC gram); adjective after the noun</sub>

**(3)** ‘The man built the boat.’

| *i-jinaŋ* | *ʒiŋ* | *in=ti* | *ʈuwaːt̪ul* | *ʒiŋ* |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| CL1-man | DEF | PST=build | boat | DEF |

/ijinaŋ ʒiŋ inti ʈuwaːt̪ul ʒiŋ/ · ‹Iyinang zhing inti ṭuwaatul zhing.›

<sub>PST is a clitic before the verb</sub>

**(4)** ‘Do you hear the thunder?’

| *nɛiʈul* | *iɽiŋ* | *ʒliluʔuʒen* | *ʒiŋ* | *liʒ* |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 2SG | hear | thunder | DEF | Q |

/nɛiʈul iɽiŋ ʒliluʔuʒen ʒiŋ liʒ/ · ‹Neiṭul iṛing zh-lilu'uzhen zhing lizh?› · rising intonation

<sub>a clause-final question particle, the word for 'if, whether' (as Russian li is both); no question gram is tracked</sub>

**(5)** ‘What does the child bring?’

| *ɡju* | *i-ɡjɛ* | *ʒiŋ* | *nʊ* |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| what | CL1-child | DEF | bring |

/ɡju iɡjɛ ʒiŋ nʊ/ · ‹Gyu igye zhing nu?›

<sub>the question word moves to the front</sub>

**(6)** ‘I do not drink the milk.’

| *ɛ* | *ɲi-ji* | *vun* | *ʒiŋ* |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1SG | NEG-drink | milk | DEF |

/ɛ ɲiji vun ʒiŋ/ · ‹E nyiyi vun zhing.›

<sub>negation is a prefix</sub>

**(7)** ‘My mother has a boat.’

| *i-jɛiwiŋ* | *ɛ* | *ʊɽaŋ* | *ʈuwaːt̪ul* | *aȴ* |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| CL1-mother | 1SG | with | boat | INDF |

/ijɛiwiŋ ɛ ʊɽaŋ ʈuwaːt̪ul aȴ/ · ‹Iyeiwing e uṛang ṭuwaatul aľ.›

<sub>possession with 'with' ('my mother (is) with a dog'; Grambank marks neither a 'have' verb nor locational possession, and the lane picked the conjunctional type); 'with' as a preposition (no COM gram)</sub>

**(8)** ‘My older brother catches three fish.’

| *i-jil̥ur* | *ɛ* | *kuʔ* | *iȴ* | *nu* |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |

<sub>no plural marker after a numeral (the marker is not yet obligatory); numeral after the noun</sub>

Abbreviations: 1 first person; 2 second person; CL1 noun class 1; DEF definite; INDF indefinite; NEG negation; PST past; Q question particle; REL relativizer; SG singular.
